cards.title: Troubleshoot a slipping P&L by reading upward, not sideways
cards.summary: Use the P&L hierarchy to locate which line above a missed target is causing the miss instead of guessing at an ads problem.
cards.use_when: Monthly or weekly review when net profit, contribution margin or gross margin misses target and you need to decide whether to cut spend, fix returns, reprice or renegotiate freight.
steps: Build the P&L as a stacked ladder: Revenue, Cost of Delivery, Gross Margin, Marketing (MEA), Contribution Margin, OPEX, EBITDA, Interest, Net Profit.
Express every line as a percentage of revenue as well as dollars, and track month-over-month movement rather than a single snapshot.

Apply the fault rule: if a target line is missed, the cause is everything above it. Missed EBITDA = OPEX, MEA or cost of delivery. Missed contribution margin = MEA or cost of delivery. Missed gross margin = cost of delivery or revenue (both gross and net).
Chase the specific lever inside the guilty line: refunds, discounts, shipping collected at checkout, landed cost, pick/pack, transaction fees, or media spend.

Set your contribution margin target by working up from the bottom: net profit target + forecast OPEX = required contribution margin, in both percent and dollars. A $1M net target with $1M OPEX requires $2M contribution margin.
Check whether revenue growth came from gross revenue or from a shrinking refund/discount allowance, since accounting software usually only surfaces net.
caveats: Contribution margin is used loosely — the source defines CM1 as product margin, CM2 as gross margin, CM3 as the revenue-minus-cost-of-delivery-minus-marketing figure; confirm which a report means.
Source is an agency operator's framing at 7–9 figure brands; percentage bands are illustrative, not benchmarks.

cards.title: Separate gross and net revenue to find hidden profit
cards.summary: Gross-to-net breakdown exposes refunds, discounts and shipping collected as the real revenue levers most accounting software hides.
cards.use_when: When revenue moved between two periods and you cannot explain it from marketing or OPEX, or when you are deciding where to hunt for margin before cutting ad spend.
steps: Pull gross revenue, refunds/chargebacks, discount allowance and shipping collected separately, per period. Shopify shows this gross-to-net view; many platforms and accounting tools (Xero, QuickBooks) show only net or a cash read.
Compare the same gross number across months and check whether the net movement came from refunds or discounts rather than new demand.

Treat each line as a lever: fewer refunds, fewer discount codes redeemed, and more shipping collected at checkout all increase net revenue without extra traffic. The source claims most stores under-collect shipping at checkout.
If a gross-to-net view is not flowing into your accounting software, have your bookkeeper reconcile it into a custom report so decisions are not made off a net-only figure.
Investigate refund-rate spikes by product and cohort before assuming a media problem, especially in fashion where the source says refund rates have been seen from 10% up to 80%.
caveats: Gross-to-net detail may require custom reporting work; the source notes this gap exists in most accounting stacks.
Raising shipping collected is a pricing/offer change — test conversion impact before rolling out.

cards.title: Custom 30–80% refund rates separately from marketing performance
cards.summary: Discounts raise the break-even ROAS non-linearly, so design offers around bundling and gift-with-purchase instead of flat price cuts.
cards.use_when: Pricing and offer decisions — planning a promo, a bundle, a gift-with-purchase, or a clearance push, and setting the media efficiency target that promo must hit.
steps: Calculate break-even ROAS before any promo: 1 ÷ gross margin percentage. At 40% gross margin the break-even ROAS is 2.5; the break-even CAC in dollars equals gross margin, so $40.

Redo the math at the discounted price with cost of goods held constant. A 30% discount taking price from $100 to $70 against $60 of cost leaves $10 gross margin, so break-even ROAS becomes 10 and break-even CAC becomes $10 — five times harder.
Use that number as a go/no-go test: if the required efficiency is physically unattainable on the platforms, the discount will not pay for itself regardless of demand uplift.

Prefer bundling: shipping and fulfillment costs do not double with a second unit (the source estimates roughly 20% inflation), so bundle gross margin percentage holds while AOV rises and more CAC can be absorbed.
Prefer gift-with-purchase on high-margin items: giving a low-cost bag (say $4 cost, displayed at $50–60) with two $100 towels forgoes $4 of margin to add $100 of revenue.
Reserve flat discounting for inventory that is not moving — the source argues break-even cash recovery beats holding dead stock.
caveats: The 20% incremental fulfillment inflation is a source estimate, not a measured benchmark; verify with your own 3PL rates.
Discounted periods should not be used to judge new-customer acquisition economics — the source advises keeping deep discounts off public acquisition offers.

cards.title: Calculate true gross margin using the full cost of delivery
cards.summary: Gross margin must include landed cost, pick/pack, shipping, transaction fees and refund/discount allowance — not just the PO price.
cards.use_when: Before setting marketing KPIs on a product, deciding whether to keep or cut a SKU, or comparing your margin to competitor pricing.
steps: Reject product margin as gross margin. If a product costs $30 and sells at $100, 70% is product margin, not gross margin.
Build the full stack: product cost, import duties/tariffs, freight to your warehouse (landed cost), pick/pack, outbound shipping, transaction fees, and a refund/discount allowance.
Transaction fees belong in cost of delivery, not OPEX, because they vary with revenue.
Remove pass-through tax from price before calculating margin.

Worked source example on a $100 apparel item: $30 product, $4 landed freight per unit, $11 shipping, $4 pick/pack, $3 transaction fee, $9 tax removed, $15 refund/discount allowance — $76 cost of delivery, giving roughly 24% gross margin instead of the assumed 70%.
Use the corrected gross margin to set the share of revenue you can spend on marketing; margin that low means a 20–25% media allocation is no longer safe.
Recompute per SKU, since margin compression from returns is product-specific.
caveats: The worked example is illustrative and deliberately extreme; your numbers will differ by category and freight method.
Refund-rate ranges vary enormously in fashion, so apply your own cohort refund data rather than a default.

cards.title: Split variable and fixed marketing costs inside the P&L
cards.summary: Media spend, influencer fees and agency retainers are variable (MEA); in-house creative teams are fixed (OPEX) — miscategorising either distorts contribution margin.
cards.use_when: Structuring your P&L for monthly review, or deciding whether to bring creative production in-house versus using agencies and freelancers.
steps: Put media spend, influencer payments, events and out-of-home into MEA — anything variable with revenue.
Classify content production by whether it is fixed or flexes with demand. A permanent in-house team is OPEX.
Recognise that creative demand flexes seasonally (flat Q1, June spike, heavy November–December), so a fixed team is underworked, overloaded and then briefly right-sized through the year.
Cover the flex with agencies or short-term hires and route those costs to MEA as variable spend; the source notes some brands put all creative in MEA, which is a legitimate brand-level choice.

Keep OPEX genuinely fixed as you scale so margin percentage expands; the source argues seven-figure founders routinely let OPEX grow faster than MEA and cost of delivery, leaving profit flat in dollars.
caveats: Treating all creative as MEA flatters gross margin but reduces comparability to prior periods; pick one convention and keep it consistent.
The margin-expansion logic assumes OPEX stays flat — it does not hold if you add headcount ahead of revenue.

cards.title: Waterfall pricing from bottom to top
cards.summary: Price by working from a contribution margin target through CAC, returns, fulfillment and COGS up to a price — then test it against competitors and cut the SKU if it fails.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product, repricing an existing one, or evaluating whether a hero SKU can carry paid acquisition.
steps: Start at the bottom with your contribution profit target, derived from your net profit target plus forecast OPEX (e.g. 10% net + 10% OPEX = 20% contribution margin target).
Add estimated CAC for that product based on existing ad account evidence.
Add a shrink allowance for returns and discounts separately (the source uses ~3% each in an example).
Add shipping and fulfillment cost from actual courier/3PL quotes, then add cost of goods.
Solve for price: Target CM + Target CAC + Return Allowance + Shipping/Fulfillment + COGS = Price.

Run competitor research against the resulting price. If everyone else sells at $30–40 and the model demands $70, decide whether a premium positioning can be sustained in a less contested tier — if not, do not sell the product.
Reject keystone pricing (2x product cost) and arbitrary multiples (3x–5x) as substitutes, since neither accounts for fulfillment costs, competitor prices or price elasticity.
caveats: The source estimates roughly 40% of startups price using keystone, a rough impression rather than a study.
CAC estimates for new products are uncertain; revisit the model once real acquisition data exists.

cards.title: Read product-level economics to beat maximize-conversions bidding
cards.summary: Per-product CAC versus contribution margin reveals which SKUs deserve paid spend, because default bidding optimises the cheapest CPA rather than the most profitable sale.
cards.use_when: Campaign structure and budget allocation decisions when a low-CPA product is absorbing spend while a higher-margin product under-sells.
steps: Build a product-level table: retail price, cost of goods, gross margin dollars, CAC, contribution margin per sale.

Source example: a $90 hoodie with $21 COGS gives $69 gross margin; at $45 CAC it yields $24 contribution. A cheaper t-shirt with $27 gross margin at $15 CAC yields $12 — half the contribution despite a lower CPA.

Recognise that maximize-conversions bidding on Meta, Google or TikTok will send spend to the lowest-CPA item, which here is the less profitable product. Switching to maximize conversion value also fails here, because the hoodie has the worse ROAS.
Fix it structurally: segment campaigns by product category using product-level economics, or split budgets so high-contribution products get deliberate spend.

Apply a cannibalisation test: if a SKU acquires at an implausibly low cost, it may sell organically without media. Cutting spend there can lift its contribution per order and free budget for products that genuinely need paid support to clear.
Revisit allocation for omni-channel and large brands where in-store or organic demand inflates apparent efficiency.
caveats: The dollar figures are a single illustrative example, not category benchmarks.
Organic-versus-paid attribution is a judgement call; avoid cutting spend on a SKU without a holdout test.

cards.title: Geo-lift testing to measure true incremental spend
cards.summary: Select control and treatment regions, hold out spend, and compare actual revenue against predicted counterfactual revenue.
cards.use_when: When platform ROAS is untrustworthy and you need to decide how much more (or less) to spend in paid media, or validate a channel's real contribution before scaling budget.
steps: Choose a control region and a treatment region with reasonably comparable demand and seasonality, and define the test window up front.
Hold out spend in the control region for the test period rather than relying on platform-reported lift.
Build a predicted counterfactual revenue for the control region from its pre-test history (and, where possible, comparable regions).
Measure the difference between actual revenue and predicted counterfactual revenue as the incremental effect of the spend.
Feed the incremental result back into CAC and break-even modelling rather than into platform-reported CPA.
Treat this as the answer to the source's core argument that attribution is unreliable and the gap between the ad account and the bank account is where brands get into trouble.
caveats: Region comparability and seasonality are the main failure modes; the source gives the design but no minimum viable region count or duration.
Results are estimates, not proof of channel-level causation, especially in small samples.

cards.title: Forecast new and returning revenue as separate models
cards.summary: New customer revenue is driven by marketing inputs; returning revenue is driven by cohort decay rates and product launches — mixing them produces a forecast nobody can act on.
cards.use_when: Annual or quarterly planning, budget setting, or when deciding how hard to push acquisition versus retention investment.
steps: Build two separate forecast models. New customer revenue: forecast marketing spend and expected new-customer CAC, then derive new customers and multiply by new-customer AOV.
Returning customer revenue: apply historical cohort decay rates to existing customer cohorts and layer on expected product launches or restock events.
Keep new-customer AOV and gross profit separate from blended AOV, since returning customers carry higher AOV and inflate blended figures.

Source illustration: $200k monthly revenue split $140k new and $60k returning; at $50k ad spend and 50% gross margin, new-customer contribution is about $20k while returning contributes roughly $27.5k after ~$2.5k of retention tooling and agency cost — i.e. most profit came from repeat buyers.
Use the split to decide whether acquisition can be subsidised by repeat profit, and how much.
caveats: The revenue split is described by the source as typical for a business of that size; it is an example, not a benchmark.
Cohort decay rates degrade if assortment, pricing or market conditions change; refresh them regularly.

cards.title: Fix CAC measurement before setting CAC targets
cards.summary: Use total ad spend divided by new customers, and pair CAC against first-purchase gross profit on new customers only.
cards.use_when: Setting acquisition targets, reviewing agency performance, or diagnosing why a 'healthy' blended CAC is not producing profit.
steps: Calculate CAC as total advertising spend over the period divided by total new customers acquired in that period — not platform CPA, which runs on attributed numbers and typically flatters the result.
Refuse channel-level CAC breakdowns; the source argues attribution makes per-channel deltas unreliable.
Pair CAC against gross profit on first purchase, not blended AOV times a possibly-wrong gross margin percentage. New customers typically have lower AOV and heavier discount-driven front-end offers.

Worked check: a $100 blended AOV at an assumed 70% gross margin looks like $70 GP and a comfortable $35 CAC — but if the new-customer AOV is really $90 and front-end discounting compresses margin, true first-purchase GP might be $50, making the CAC target wrong.
Answer 'what is a good CAC?' as a non-question: a $100 CAC against $10,000 first-order GP is excellent; a $100 CAC against $20 GP is a loss. Judge CAC only relative to first-purchase gross profit.
caveats: Attribution-free CAC is a deliberate simplification; channel decisions then rely on experiments such as geo-lift.
Requires clean new-versus-returning customer tagging in your platform and analytics.

cards.title: Separate new-customer and returning-customer profit contribution
cards.summary: Compute contribution margin on new and returning revenue separately to see where the business actually makes money.
cards.use_when: Deciding budget split between acquisition and retention, or when a founder wants to increase ad spend but the profit source is unclear.
steps: Split monthly revenue into new-customer revenue and returning-customer revenue.
For new customers: new revenue minus ad spend, minus cost of delivery/gross margin, equals new-customer profit contribution.
For returning customers: returning revenue minus gross margin cost, minus retention tooling (email/SMS platform) and any retention agency, equals returning-customer profit contribution.

Source illustration: $140k new revenue minus $50k ad spend at 50% gross margin gives ~$20k; $60k returning revenue minus ~$2.5k tooling and agency gives ~$27.5k — the smaller revenue stream produced the larger profit.
Use the returning-customer profit pool to judge how aggressively you can subsidise new-customer acquisition, and whether increasing new-customer spend is self-funding.
Route the result into retention planning: repeat purchase is driven by product, experience and brand, not by media spend.
caveats: Requires reliable customer-cohort tagging and defensible gross-margin figures.
Retention tooling and agency costs vary widely; use your actual invoices.

cards.title: Measure 90/180-day LTGP, not open-ended LTV
cards.summary: Restrict customer value to a fixed window and use gross profit rather than revenue so acquisition bids are grounded.
cards.use_when: Setting maximum allowable CAC for CPG, fashion or subscription models where first-order profitability is negative or thin.
steps: Cap the measurement window — the source recommends 90-day or 180-day windows because LTV keeps rising as you extend the horizon, even where it asymptotes.

Compute lifetime gross profit (LTGP), not revenue-based LTV. Many tools report LTV as revenue; in e-commerce the distinction matters because software-style LTV is often close to gross profit while e-commerce LTV is not.
Compare LTGP against CAC to establish payback. The source notes most agencies run a 3–6 month CAC payback period, and CPG brands frequently lose money on first purchase.
Expect competitors with larger repeat value to outbid you at auction; if your LTGP is thin, paying their CAC level is not viable.
Use the window-consistent LTGP to set the ceiling bid, then check it against the 90/180-day actuals before scaling.
caveats: Window choice changes the answer; compare cohorts measured over the same window only.
Cohort LTGP is backward-looking and can overstate value for brands with changing retention.

cards.title: Ring-fence OPEX to protect margin while scaling
cards.summary: In e-commerce the growth lever is marketing, not headcount or software, so overinflating OPEX flattens profit as revenue grows.
cards.use_when: Budget review when revenue is growing but net profit is flat in dollars, or when deciding whether to hire, add software or upsize an office.
steps: Define OPEX as anything not in cost of delivery or marketing. The three big buckets are people, software and office/fulfillment space.

Keep true fulfillment costs — 3PL, warehouse, and warehouse staff doing pick/pack/ship — inside cost of delivery. Allocate warehouse staff per order (source example: $400/day ÷ 100 packages = $4/order) and have your bookkeeper tag and reclassify them into a custom P&L so gross margin stays accurate.
Keep everyone not directly fulfilling orders (head of marketing, head of operations) in OPEX.

Model the intended scaling shape: OPEX flat, marketing and cost of delivery rising with revenue, so profit expands as a percentage. Watch for OPEX rising faster than revenue, which leaves profit flat.

Be sceptical of 'reinvest in the business' leading to hiring and software that do not drive revenue. Marketing is the revenue lever; people set the skill ceiling but poor hires inflate cost without output.
Put interest expense below EBITDA, never in OPEX — it is financing leverage, and buyers evaluating EBITDA zero out loans.
caveats: The source argues OPEX should stay near-fixed, which assumes no step changes in headcount or systems; treat it as a discipline target, not an absolute.
The source concedes seven-figure brands often lack the skill to hire top talent, so the advice is to delay heavy people investment rather than never hire.

cards.title: Use EBITDA and net profit as distinct decision numbers
cards.summary: EBITDA shows earnings capacity before financing; net profit shows what the owner actually keeps after interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to take on inventory financing, setting owner distributions, or preparing numbers for a buyer or investor.
steps: Run the P&L ladder with percentages: $100 revenue, $40 cost of delivery, $60 gross margin, $20 MEA, $40 contribution margin, $20 OPEX, $20 EBITDA, then interest below the line, then net profit.
Place interest repayments below EBITDA, not in OPEX. The source flags interest in OPEX as a common error in seven and eight-figure P&Ls.
Use EBITDA to judge the business's earning power independent of loans — the number a buyer would look at after zeroing debt.
Use net profit to judge actual cash-generating performance after debt service, which matters more for operational decisions inside an e-commerce brand that leans on loans for inventory and media.
Track both over time as percentages so you can see compression early, and remember net profit is not cash flow — the source notes they diverge in e-commerce.
caveats: The percentages in the example are illustrative, not target benchmarks for any category.
EBITDA ignores working capital swings that dominate e-commerce cash.
